pages.name: The complex plane
pages.text: A complex number has two parts, a real part and a `j` part, so it needs two directions: the number line across for the real part, and a line of its own through 0, straight up, for the `j` part. This is the coordinate plane with its axes renamed: the [[complex plane]], also called an [[Argand diagram]].

pages.alt: The complex plane: real across, j up. 3 + j2 sits 3 across, 2 up. −2 − j3 sits 2 left, 3 down. 3 plus j2: 3 across, 2 up. minus 2 minus j3: 2 left, 3 down.

pages.name: Read a dot
pages.task: Which number does this dot mark?
pages.why: Across first. The dot is 2 to the left of 0, so its real part is `−2`. Then up. It is 3 up, so its `j` part is 3. The dot marks `−2 + j3`.

pages.name: Four quarters
pages.text: The two axes cut the plane into four quarters, and complex numbers sit in all of them. `4 − j3` is in the bottom right, 4 across and 3 down. With no `j` part, `6 + j0` lies on the real axis; with no real part, `0 + j4` lies on the `j` axis.

pages.name: (2 + j3) + (4 − j1)
pages.task: Work out `(2 + j3) + (4 − j1)`. After Check, the second arrow slides onto the first to show your answer.
pages.why: Real parts: `2 + 4 = 6`. The `j` parts: `3 + (−1) = 2`. So the sum is `6 + j2`. Laid on the first arrow's tip, the second arrow finishes 6 across and 2 up.

pages.name: Lengths do not add
pages.text: The sum adds the parts, not the lengths. Take `4 + j0`, an arrow 4 long, and `0 + j3`, an arrow 3 long. Their lengths add to `4 + 3 = 7`.

pages.alt: The plane, real across and j up. First arrow to 4 plus j0, second arrow to 0 plus j3. Laid tip to tail they finish at 4 plus j3. (4 plus j0) plus (0 plus j3): 4 plus j3. Length of the sum: the square root of (4 squared plus 3 squared): 5. Lengths added: 4 plus 3: 7.

pages.name: (−3 + j2) + (1 − j4)
pages.why: Real parts: `−3 + 1 = −2`. The `j` parts: `2 + (−4) = −2`. The sum is `−2 − j2`, in the bottom left quarter.

pages.name: Taking away
pages.text: Taking away is adding the opposite. Multiplying by `−1` turns an arrow through 180°, the same length pointing the other way, so `−(2 + j1)` is `−2 − j1`. Both parts change sign.
